hmmt-nov-2024-thm-01.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-01.body:
The top-left $2\times2$ block already contains $T$ and $A$ (at its top-left and bottom-right cells), so the cell to the right of $T$ is $L$ or $C$ and the cell below $T$ is the other one. Similarly the bottom-right block contains $L$ (top-left) and $C$ (bottom-right), so its other two cells are $T$ and $A$.

Take the top row to start $T,L$ (so the cell below $T$ is $C$). Then row $1$ ends with $C,A$ in some order and row $2$ (which is $C,A,\_,\_$) ends with $T,L$. Column $3$ already has $L$ in row $3$, so row $2$'s third cell is $T$ and its fourth is $L$. Column $4$ now has $L$ and $C$, so the top-right cell is $A$ and the cell next to it is $C$. Row $3$ is $\_,\_,L,\_$ and column $4$ already has $A,L,C$ in rows $1,2,4$, so its last cell must be $T$. Column $1$ already has $T,C$, so row $3$ continues $A,C$: row $3$ is $A,C,L,T$. Row $4$ is then forced to be $L,T,A,C$:
$$\begin{array}{cccc}T&L&C&A\\C&A&T&L\\A&C&L&T\\L&T&A&C\end{array}$$
So this choice leads to exactly one filling. Starting with $T,C$ instead gives the transpose of this grid (reflection in the main diagonal fixes the given letters), again exactly one filling:
$$\begin{array}{cccc}T&C&A&L\\L&A&C&T\\C&T&L&A\\A&L&T&C\end{array}$$
Total: $2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-02.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-02.body:
Let $s(m)$ denote the digit sum of $m$ and let $n$ be the pile size.

If $n=10^k$ ($k\ge1$), split it into two equal piles of $5\cdot10^{k-1}$, each with digit sum $5<7$; so $s(n)\ne1$. If $n=10^{i_1}+\cdots+10^{i_s}$ with $2\le s=s(n)\le12$ (written with its digit units), we can split these $s$ powers of ten into two groups of at most $6$ terms each, giving two piles with digit sums at most $6$; this also fails. Hence $s(n)\ge13$, and the smallest such $n$ is $49$ (every number below $49$ has digit sum at most $12$, e.g. $39$).

$n=49$ works: for any split $a+b=49$ the units digits sum to $9$ (they sum to $9$ or $19$, and $19>18$ is impossible), so there is no carry and $s(a)+s(b)=s(49)=13$. Then one of $s(a),s(b)$ is at least $7$.

**Answer: 49**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-03.title: Areas
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-03.body:
The circumradius of $CAT$ is $CI=2$, so its side is $2\sqrt3$ and its area is $3\sqrt3$. Triangle $ELK$ has half that area, so the three corner triangles $CEK$, $AEL$, $TLK$ (congruent by the rotation about $I$) share the remaining half: $[CEK]=\frac16\cdot3\sqrt3=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$. Then
$$\frac12\,CE\cdot CK\sin60^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ CE\cdot CK=2.$$
By the rotation symmetry, $AE=CK$, so $CE+CK=CE+EA=CA=2\sqrt3$. Hence $CK(2\sqrt3-CK)=2$, i.e. $CK^2-2\sqrt3CK+2=0$ and $CK=\sqrt3\pm1$. The minimum is $\sqrt3-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3-1$**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-03.title: Right triangle
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-03.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $CT$; then $IM$ is the apothem, $IM=1$ and $CM=\sqrt3$. The areas satisfy $[CAT]=2[ELK]$, so the circumradii ratio is $\sqrt2$ and $KI=\frac{CI}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$. Triangle $KIM$ has a right angle at $M$ ($IM\perp CT$), so $KM=\sqrt{KI^2-IM^2}=\sqrt{2-1}=1$. Hence $CK=CM\pm KM=\sqrt3\pm1$, with minimum $\sqrt3-1$.

**Answer: $\sqrt3-1$**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-04.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-04.body:
None of $i,t,e\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ is divisible by $5$, so $5\nmid ite$. Pair the term for $i$ with the term for $5-i$ (same $t,e$): since $(5-i)te\equiv-ite\pmod5$ and $ite\not\equiv0$, the two remainders add to $5$, so
$$\left\lfloor\frac{ite}{5}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{(5-i)te}{5}\right\rfloor=\frac{ite+(5-i)te}{5}-1.$$
Summing over all $64$ terms (i.e. $32$ pairs),
$$\sum\left\lfloor\frac{ite}{5}\right\rfloor=\frac15\sum_{i,t,e}ite-32=\frac{(1+2+3+4)^3}{5}-32=200-32=168.$$

**Answer: 168**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-05.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-05.body:
Let the days on which Alf eats be $a_1>a_2>\cdots>a_m$. The rule says that after eating on day $a_{i+1}$ the next eating day $a_i$ satisfies $a_i\ge2a_{i+1}$, i.e. $a_{i+1}\le\lfloor a_i/2\rfloor$. Starting from $a_1\le100$:
$$a_2\le50,\ a_3\le25,\ a_4\le12,\ a_5\le6,\ a_6\le3,\ a_7\le1,$$
so $m\le7$ and the total is at most $100+50+25+12+6+3+1=197$.

This is achieved by eating on days $1,3,6,12,25,50,100$: consecutive eating days differ in the required way ($3\ge2\cdot1$, $6\ge2\cdot3$, $12\ge2\cdot6$, $25\ge2\cdot12$, $50\ge2\cdot25$, $100\ge2\cdot50$). The maximum is $197$.

**Answer: 197**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-06.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-06.body:
The vertices in order are $F,E,L,D,S,P,A,R$, so $D$ and $R$ are opposite and $DR$ is a diameter; by symmetry $I$ lies on it. The diameter $DR$ is parallel to the chord $FL$, so $ID\parallel FL$ and $\angle FLI=\angle LID=\angle FIL$ (alternate angles, then the given equality). Hence triangle $FIL$ is isosceles with $FI=FL$. In the same way $AI=AS$.

$FLSA$ is a square (alternate vertices of the octagon), so $FL=AS=FA$. Therefore $FI=FA=AI$ and triangle $FIA$ is equilateral. The line $RI$ is its axis of symmetry, so $\angle AIR=\frac12\cdot60^\circ=30^\circ$. Also $AR$ and $RF$ are symmetric about $RD$, so $\angle ARI=\frac12\cdot135^\circ=67.5^\circ$.

In triangle $IAR$: $\angle IAR=180^\circ-30^\circ-67.5^\circ=82.5^\circ$.

**Answer: $82.5^\circ$**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-07.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-07.body:
After any sequence of moves, the leftmost nonempty jug never holds more ounces than the second leftmost one (all jugs start equal, and each move preserves this).

**Jasper can guarantee $31$.** As long as at least two jugs are nonempty, Jasper removes all but one ounce from the leftmost jug. Then Rose can only ever take one ounce from one or two jugs at a time, so on each of Jasper's turns the first jug again holds more than one ounce. Eventually Rose is forced to take one ounce from jug Y and at most one ounce from jug Z, leaving at least $31$ ounces of Quart Z for Jasper.

**Jasper cannot guarantee $32$.** If only jugs Y and Z remain on Rose's turn, she can take at least one ounce from Z. So Jasper could collect all $32$ only if Rose is forced to empty jug X without touching Y or Z, so that Jasper can then take all of Z in one move; that requires Rose to empty jugs W and X simultaneously. But Rose could instead just empty W alone (the leftmost jug), contradiction.

So the maximum Jasper can guarantee is $31$.

**Answer: 31**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-08.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-08.body:
We have $\operatorname{Top}(r,s)=\frac{r}{\gcd(r,s)}$.

**Claim:** $\operatorname{Top}(a,z)=\operatorname{Top}(z,a-1)$ iff there are positive integers $d,e$ with $e\mid d^2-1$, $a=d^2$ and $z=de$.

($\Leftarrow$) $e\mid d^2-1$ gives $\gcd(d,e)=1$, so $\gcd(d^2,de)=d$ and $\operatorname{Top}(a,z)=\frac{d^2}{d}=d$; also $\gcd(de,d^2-1)=e$ (as $\gcd(d,d^2-1)=1$), so $\operatorname{Top}(z,a-1)=\frac{de}{e}=d$.

($\Rightarrow$) Let $d=\gcd(a,z)$, $e=\gcd(z,a-1)$. Then $\gcd(d,e)$ divides both $a$ and $a-1$, so it is $1$. The equation $\frac ad=\frac ze$ gives $\frac az=\frac de$ with $\frac de$ already in lowest terms, so $a/d=d$ and $z/d=e$, i.e. $a=d^2$, $z=de$, and $e\mid a-1=d^2-1$.

Now $200\le d^2\le300$ gives $d\in\{15,16,17\}$, and for each $d$ every divisor $e$ of $d^2-1$ gives exactly one pair. The number of pairs is $\tau(224)+\tau(255)+\tau(288)=12+8+18=38$ (since $224=2^5\cdot7$, $255=3\cdot5\cdot17$, $288=2^5\cdot3^2$).

**Answer: 38**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-09.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-09.body:
Split the grid into $36$ disjoint $3\times3$ blocks, each containing exactly one ruby cell. Compare two adjacent blocks (say $A$ left of $C$): sliding a $3\times3$ window from $A$ to $C$ shows that the ruby in $C$ sits at the same height as the ruby in $A$, only shifted horizontally by $0$ or $\pm1,\pm2$ cells, and similarly for vertically adjacent blocks. In a $2\times2$ arrangement of blocks the two shifts along each pair of opposite sides are equal, and it is impossible to have both a nontrivial horizontal shift and a nontrivial vertical shift, since then some $3\times3$ window would contain $0$ or $2$ rubies.

Consequently, over the whole grid either all shifts are horizontal only, or vertical only, or absent: all rubies lie in six equally spaced rows or in six equally spaced columns, and every such configuration is valid.

Count the configurations with all rubies in six equally spaced rows: the six rows are $r,r+3,\dots,r+15$ with $r\in\{1,2,3\}$ ($3$ ways), and in each of these rows the rubies occupy every third cell, with $3$ choices of offset per row: $3\cdot3^6=3^7$. By symmetry $3^7$ configurations have all rubies in six equally spaced columns. Those counted twice have rubies in six rows and six columns (the rubies sit at all $36$ intersections): $3\cdot3=9$.

Total: $2\cdot3^7-9=4374-9=4365$.

**Answer: 4365**

hmmt-nov-2024-thm-10.title: Solution
hmmt-nov-2024-thm-10.body:
Since $PABCD$ is cyclic and $AD\parallel BC$, $ABCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid: $AB=CD=a$ and the diagonals $AC=BD=b$. Ptolemy in $ABCD$: $b^2=AD\cdot BC+a^2=3850+a^2$.

Let $PA=3x$, $PD=4x$, $PB=5y$, $PC=6y$. Ptolemy in $PABC$ and in $PBCD$:
$$5yb=3x\cdot55+6ya,\qquad 6yb=5ya+4x\cdot55.$$
Solving this linear system for $yb$ and $ya$: $ya=10x$ and $yb=45x$, so $b=\frac92a$. Substituting into $b^2=3850+a^2$ gives $\frac{81}{4}a^2-a^2=3850$, so $a^2=200$, $a=10\sqrt2$, $b=45\sqrt2$.

Next, in triangle $ABD$: $\cos\angle ABD=\frac{a^2+b^2-70^2}{2ab}=\frac{200+4050-4900}{1800}=-\frac{13}{36}$. As $P$ and $B$ are on opposite sides of $AD$ on the circle, $\angle APD=180^\circ-\angle ABD$ and $\cos\angle APD=\frac{13}{36}$. The law of cosines in triangle $PAD$:
$$4900=9x^2+16x^2-2\cdot12x^2\cdot\frac{13}{36}=\frac{49}{3}x^2,$$
so $x^2=300$ and $x=10\sqrt3$. Finally $y=\frac{10x}{a}=\frac{10\cdot10\sqrt3}{10\sqrt2}=5\sqrt6$ and $PB=5y=25\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $25\sqrt6$**
